title: Decision Tree
content:
A decision tree is a tree-shaped classification model in which every internal node tests one attribute of the input, every branch represents the outcome of that test, and every leaf node assigns a class label. To classify a new example, start at the root and follow the branch matching the example's attribute values, node after node, until a leaf is reached.

This is nothing more than a nested sequence of if-else questions applied to the attributes of an example.

Entropy
content:
For a set $S$ containing examples from $c$ classes, entropy measures how mixed or impure the set is:
\[
H(S) = -\sum_{i=1}^{c} p_i \log_2 p_i
\]
where $p_i$ is the proportion of examples in $S$ belonging to class $i$.

This is the same weighted-average-of-surprise idea used in information theory.

Quick Reference: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] $_2 2 =
Information Gain
content:
Information Gain measures how much entropy is reduced by splitting a set $S$ on attribute $A$:
\[
\text{Gain}(S,A) = H(S) - \sum_{v \in Values(A)} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} H(S_v)
\]
where $S_v$ is the subset of $S$ for which attribute $A$ has value $v$.

Think of it as the total entropy minus a weighted average of the entropies of the resulting pieces.

Choosing the Splitting Attribute: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Compute
ID3 Algorithm
content:
\textbf{Input:} A set of training examples $S$ a target class attribute and a set of candidate attributes $A$

\textbf{Output:} A decision tree that classifies the training examples

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Create a root node for the tree.
\item If all examples in $S$ belong to the same class $c$ label the root with $c$ and stop.
\item If the attribute set $A$ is empty label the root with the majority class in $S$ and stop.
\item Otherwise compute Information Gain for every remaining attribute in $A$ and select the attribute $A^\ast$ with the highest gain as the decision attribute for the root.
\item For each possible value $v$ of $A^\ast$ add a new branch below the root for $A^\ast = v$ and let $S_v$ be the subset of examples with $A^\ast = v$.
\item If $S_v$ is empty attach a leaf labeled with the majority class of $S$ below this branch.
\item Otherwise attach the subtree obtained by recursively applying steps 2 to 6 to $S_v$ using $A - \{A^\ast\}$ as the remaining attribute set.
\item Return the root node.
\end{enumerate}

ID3 Stopping Conditions (Base Cases): enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
content:
\textbf{ID3 Stopping Conditions (Base Cases):}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item All remaining examples belong to the same class $\Rightarrow$ create a leaf with that class
\item No attributes are left to split on $\Rightarrow$ create a leaf with the majority class
\item A branch has no matching examples $\Rightarrow$ create a leaf with the majority class of the parent set
\item Otherwise pick the attribute with the highest Information Gain and recurse
\end{enumerate}

title: Bayes' Theorem
content:
Bayes' Theorem relates the probability of a hypothesis $H$ given evidence $E$ to the reverse conditional probability:
\[
P(H \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}
\]
where $P(H)$ is the \textbf{prior}, $P(E \mid H)$ is the \textbf{likelihood}, $P(E)$ is the \textbf{evidence probability}, and $P(H \mid E)$ is the \textbf{posterior}.

This is simply the definition of conditional probability rearranged and applied in the reverse direction.

Naive Bayes Classification Rule
Naive Bayes Classifier Algorithm
content:
\textbf{Input:} A training set with attributes $A_1,\ldots,A_n$, a class attribute $C$, and one test instance

\textbf{Output:} The predicted class label for the test instance

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item For each class $C_k$, compute the prior $P(C_k) = \dfrac{\text{count}(C_k)}{\text{total examples}}$.
\item For each attribute $A_i$ and each class $C_k$, compute the likelihood $P(A_i \mid C_k)$ from the training data.
\item For the test instance, compute the score $P(C_k)\prod_i P(A_i \mid C_k)$ for every class $C_k$ using the instance's attribute values.
\item Predict the class $C_k$ with the highest score.
\end{enumerate}

The Zero-Probability Problem: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] If an
content:
\textbf{The Zero-Probability Problem:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item If an attribute value never occurs with a class in training data, its likelihood is $0$
\item A single zero likelihood forces the entire product (and hence the score) to $0$, as seen for Apple in Example 2.17
\item This can wrongly rule out a class even when the other evidence supports it
\item Fix: \textbf{Laplace smoothing} adds a small count to every likelihood so no probability is ever exactly zero
\end{enumerate}

title: Artificial Neural Network
content: An artificial neural network (ANN) is a computational model inspired by the brain, made of simple processing units called neurons that are connected together. Each connection carries a weight, and the network learns by adjusting these weights so that a given input produces the desired output.

title: Perceptron
Common Activation Functions
Perceptron Output Computation
content:
\textbf{Input:} input values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, weights $w_1,\ldots,w_n$, bias $b$, an activation function $f$

\textbf{Output:} the perceptron's output $y$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Compute the weighted sum $\text{net} = \sum_i w_i x_i + b$.
\item Apply the activation function: $y = f(\text{net})$.
\item Return $y$.
\end{enumerate}

Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
Forward Propagation Algorithm
content:
\textbf{Input:} input vector $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, weights and biases for the hidden layer and the output layer, an activation function $f$

\textbf{Output:} the network's final output $y$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item For each hidden neuron $h_j$, compute $\text{net}_{h_j} = \sum_i w_{ij}x_i + b_j$ and then $h_j = f(\text{net}_{h_j})$.
\item Using the hidden outputs $h_j$ as inputs, compute $\text{net}_{y} = \sum_j v_j h_j + b_{\text{out}}$.
\item Compute the final output $y = f(\text{net}_y)$.
\item Return $y$.
\end{enumerate}

Why This Network Matters: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Checking
content:
\textbf{Why This Network Matters:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Checking all four input combinations gives outputs $0,1,1,0$ for $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$
\item This is exactly the \textbf{XOR} function, which a single perceptron can never compute (see the keypoint after Example 2.21)
\item $h_1$ behaves like an OR gate and $h_2$ behaves like an AND gate; the output combines them as "$h_1$ true AND $h_2$ false"
\item This is the classic illustration of why \textbf{hidden layers} give neural networks more power than a single perceptron
\end{enumerate}

title: Hyperplane
content:
A hyperplane is the decision boundary that separates two classes in feature space. In two dimensions it is simply a line, defined by:
\[
w \cdot x + b = 0
\]
where $w$ is the weight vector (normal to the hyperplane) and $b$ is the bias term.

title: Margin and Support Vectors
Properties of the SVM Decision Function
SVM Classification Algorithm
content:
\textbf{Input:} weight vector $w$, bias $b$, and a test point $x$

\textbf{Output:} predicted class label $+1$ or $-1$ for $x$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Compute the dot product $w \cdot x$.
\item Add the bias: $\text{score} = w \cdot x + b$.
\item If $\text{score} > 0$ predict class $+1$; if $\text{score} < 0$ predict class $-1$; if $\text{score} = 0$ the point lies on the hyperplane.
\item Return the predicted class.
\end{enumerate}

Margin Width Formula
content:
Once the SVM has found the optimal $w$, the width of the margin (distance between the two dashed boundary lines) is:
\[
\text{Margin} = \frac{2}{\|w\|}, \qquad \|w\| = \sqrt{w_1^2 + w_2^2 + \cdots + w_n^2}
\]

title: Distance from a Point to the Hyperplane
content:
The perpendicular distance from any point $x$ to the hyperplane $w\cdot x + b = 0$ is:
\[
d = \frac{|w \cdot x + b|}{\|w\|}
\]

This is simply the point-to-line distance formula the students already know from coordinate geometry, extended to vector notation.

SVM Summary: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] A smaller $\|w\|$
content:
\textbf{SVM Summary:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item A \textbf{smaller} $\|w\|$ gives a \textbf{larger} margin — this is exactly what SVM training optimizes for
\item Only the support vectors (score $=0$ direction, i.e. the closest points) affect $w$ and $b$; all other points can change freely without moving the hyperplane
\item For data that is \textbf{not} linearly separable in its original features, the \textbf{kernel trick} maps points into a higher-dimensional space where a separating hyperplane does exist — the calculations themselves stay the same dot-product-and-sign process shown above, just in the transformed space
\end{enumerate}

title: Overfitting
content: A model overfits when it fits the training data too closely including its noise and random fluctuations so that it performs very well on training data but poorly on new unseen data. In decision trees, this happens when the tree grows too many branches trying to perfectly classify every single training example.

Signs of Overfitting: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Training accuracy
Pruning
content:
Pruning is the process of removing branches or subtrees from a decision tree that add complexity without improving (or that even hurt) accuracy on unseen data. \textbf{Pre-pruning} stops tree growth early using a stopping condition. \textbf{Post-pruning} grows the full tree first and then removes subtrees afterward, checking accuracy on a separate validation set.

This is the same "simplify the model, don't just fit every last training point" idea behind avoiding an unnecessarily high-degree curve fit in regression.

title: Reduced Error Pruning
content:
\textbf{Input:} a fully grown decision tree $T$, a validation dataset $V$ separate from the training data

\textbf{Output:} a pruned decision tree $T'$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Compute the accuracy of $T$ on $V$.
\item For each internal node $n$ (starting near the leaves and working upward), temporarily replace the subtree rooted at $n$ with a leaf labeled by the majority class of the training examples reaching $n$.
\item Evaluate the accuracy of this modified tree on $V$.
\item If the accuracy on $V$ does not decrease, keep the replacement permanently (prune the subtree); otherwise restore the original subtree.
\item Repeat steps 2 to 4 for every internal node until no further pruning improves or maintains validation accuracy.
\item Return the final pruned tree $T'$.
\end{enumerate}

Pre-Pruning vs Post-Pruning: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Pre-pruning is
content:
\textbf{Pre-Pruning vs Post-Pruning:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item \textbf{Pre-pruning} is faster since the tree never grows too large, but risks stopping too early (underfitting)
\item \textbf{Post-pruning} is more reliable since it evaluates the effect of removing each subtree directly on validation data
\item Pruning always trades a small amount of training accuracy for better generalization to new data
\end{enumerate}

title: Confusion Matrix
Classifier Evaluation Metrics
Computing Classifier Metrics
content:
\textbf{Input:} confusion matrix counts $TP$, $FP$, $FN$, $TN$

\textbf{Output:} Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Compute $\text{Accuracy} = \dfrac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$.
\item Compute $\text{Precision} = \dfrac{TP}{TP+FP}$.
\item Compute $\text{Recall} = \dfrac{TP}{TP+FN}$.
\item Compute $\text{F1-score} = \dfrac{2\times\text{Precision}\times\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}$.
\item Return all four values.
\end{enumerate}

Choosing the Right Metric: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Accuracy
content:
\textbf{Choosing the Right Metric:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item \textbf{Accuracy} can be misleading when classes are imbalanced, as seen in Example 2.42
\item \textbf{Precision} matters most when false positives are costly (e.g. spam filtering)
\item \textbf{Recall} matters most when false negatives are costly (e.g. disease detection)
\item \textbf{F1-score} is used when a single balance between Precision and Recall is needed
\end{enumerate}

title: Linear Regression
content:
Linear regression models the relationship between one input attribute $x$ and a continuous output $y$ by fitting a straight line:
\[
\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x
\]
where $b_1$ is the slope (how much $y$ changes per unit change in $x$) and $b_0$ is the intercept (the predicted value when $x=0$).

title: Least Squares Method
content:
The best-fitting line is the one that minimizes the sum of squared differences between the actual values $y_i$ and the predicted values $\hat{y}_i$. The coefficients that achieve this minimum are:
\[
b_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})^2}, \qquad b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}
\]
where $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ are the means of the $x$ and $y$ values.

This is the same mean-and-deviation idea used when computing variance, just applied to two variables together instead of one.

title: Simple Linear Regression (Least Squares)
content:
\textbf{Input:} training points $(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)$, and a new value $x_{\text{new}}$ to predict

\textbf{Output:} coefficients $b_0$, $b_1$, and the predicted value $\hat{y}_{\text{new}}$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Compute the means $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i$ and $\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i y_i$.
\item Compute $\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})$ and $\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})^2$.
\item Compute the slope $b_1 = \dfrac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})^2}$.
\item Compute the intercept $b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}$.
\item Form the regression equation $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x$.
\item Substitute $x_{\text{new}}$ into the equation to get $\hat{y}_{\text{new}}$.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Reading a Regression Line:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item $b_1$ (slope) tells us how much $y$ increases for every one-unit increase in $x$
\item $b_0$ (intercept) is only meaningful as the predicted $y$ when $x=0$
\item Predictions far outside the range of the original $x$ values (extrapolation) are less reliable
\end{enumerate}

title: Logistic Regression
Logistic Regression Decision Rule
Logistic Regression Classification
content:
\textbf{Input:} weights $w$, bias $b$, a test point $x$, decision threshold (default $0.5$)

\textbf{Output:} predicted class label ($0$ or $1$) and probability $P$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Compute $\text{net} = w\cdot x + b$.
\item Compute $P = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-\text{net}}}$.
\item If $P \ge 0.5$ predict class $1$; otherwise predict class $0$.
\item Return the predicted class and $P$.
\end{enumerate}

Linear Regression vs Logistic Regression: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
content:
\textbf{Linear Regression vs Logistic Regression:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Linear regression predicts a \textbf{continuous} value directly as $b_0+b_1x$
\item Logistic regression predicts a \textbf{probability} between $0$ and $1$ by passing $w\cdot x+b$ through the sigmoid function
\item Both are built from the same linear combination of attributes; only the final step (identity vs sigmoid) differs
\item Logistic regression is used for classification, not for predicting numeric quantities
\end{enumerate}
